--- title: Time to Migrate this Blog from *Distill* to *Quarto* subtitle: Mastering Quarto Markdown for literate programming, technical writing, and web publishing date: 2023-10-01 date-modified: last-modified categories: - quarto - dataviz draft: false freeze: false abstract: | A post about literate programming in general and Quarto formats in particular where I document migrating this personal blog from [Distill](https://rstudio.github.io/distill/) to [Quarto](https://quarto.org/). Compared to *J.J. Allaire's Distill for R Markdown*, **Posit® Quarto Markdown** uses a new templating system built on top of [Bootstrap v5.3.1](https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.3/customize/overview/) with new page layout features, extended export formats, and more flexible publishing workflows. This post briefly outlines my process for creating a custom Bootstrap theme for this revamped website, and few design tweaks I made along the way. --- ::: {.cell .column-screen classe='mb-4'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.aside .shaded .p-2 .mt-md-n5 .mb-md-3} No other reason for this map but to showcase Quarto's new content layout features -- and well, I {{< bi heart size=xs >}} Russian topographic maps. Check out Soviet-era [cartography](https://www.sovietmaps.com/), it is stunning work. This margin note uses a custom `DIV` with CSS classes `{.aside .shaded .mt-md-n5}` making use of Boostrap's new **negative margins** utilities and grid breakpoints. ::: With the release of **Quarto 1.4**, markdown-based publishing is gaining popularity, way beyond the scientific community. Multilingual text-based documents (such as **Emacs org-mode**, **Rmarkdown** and **Jupyter** notebooks) that combine executable code chunks with formatted prose greatly simplify the process of drafting, iterating, compiling, documenting, sharing and reproducing computable research experiments. Old-time researchers and engineers have long used **Emacs `Org-Mode`** (along with its wild hordes of keyboard shortcuts) to achieve similar results thanks to *Eric Schulte*'s incredible **Babel** extension [see @schulte2012] and to *John MacFarlane*'s [Pandoc](https://pandoc.org/) document converter library -- but nowadays Quarto makes use of more efficient script parsers and optimized runtime engines (Sass, Deno, V8) as well as **in-browser real-time rendering of documents**. In the process of migrating old articles and code notebooks to the new Quarto markdown syntax, I used this post as a template to build a complete Bootstrap theme for the revamped website. This article helped me finetune content placement and notebook execution. Feel free to reuse my `www/theme-labs.scss` Sass file and other tidbits[^1][^2]. [^1]: For folks born this century, to **babel** (elips) or to **sweave** (R) is the process of compiling text documents that include both static markup and compile-time executable scripts. ![](Donald-Knuth.jpg){.img-rounded width="10em"} The concept of **Literate programming** was introduced in 1984 by the mathematician [Donald Knuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Knuth) and was widely popularized thereafter in the engineering community thanks to [org-mode](https://orgmode.org/worg/org-contrib/babel/uses.html) in the Emacs editor. ![](Carsten-Dominik.jpg){.img-rounded width="10em"} Emacs **`Org-Mode`** was created by the astronomer [Carsten Dominik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Org-mode#:~:text=Org%20Mode%20was%20created%20by,mode%20by%20default%20since%202006) in 2003 and remains to this day one of the most used and madly loved note-taking and GTD (Get-Things-Done) tools, with many of its functionality (agenda, tags, etc.) yet to be ported to any markdown engine. [^2]: Only keyboard, Baby! ![](real-programmers.png){.lightbox} # CSS Grid System One of Quarto's many great features is the full flexibility of the Bootstrap v5.3 grid system, with a few handy classes to help precisely position content in a document or web page, in particular: - 2 predefined (column-based) page layouts: - `page-layout: full` (home page) - `page-layout: article` (this document), and - 6 column classes to control content width (shown below) - 2 margin classes to shift content into the left or right column (like that XKCD comics): - `
`, and - `` - 8 classes to overflow content into the left or right margin For example I use Quarto `{.column-screen}` CSS class to place a flushed banner directly below the post header section, as a way to highlight static or dynamic content. Here is the R code chunk to achieve this, which generates a `

Read on, tips below!", labelOptions=labelOptions(textsize="1rem")) ``` Grid sizing and spacing are defined in `_quarto.yml` and may also be modified on a per-document basis, for example by setting: ```md #| filename: ./_quarto.yml #| eval: false grid: body-width: 900px sidebar-width: 160px margin-width: 240px gutter-width: 2em ``` There are new Quarto CSS classes to help control content width and placement. ::: {.column-body .striped .mb-2} `.column-body` ::: ::: {.column-body-outset .striped .mb-2} `.column-body-outset` ::: ::: {.column-page .striped .mb-2} `.column-page` ::: ::: {.column-page-inset .striped .mb-2} `.column-page-inset` ::: ::: {.column-screen .striped .mb-2} `.column-screen` ::: ::: {.column-screen-inset-shaded .mb-4} `.column-screen-inset-shaded` ::: Finally any layout is achievable using stackable `

Scheme Choosing a color scheme is relatively easy -- for example you can start from your favorite photo or graphic and upload it to one of the many on-line **color palette generators** to extract base and accent colors. Below I selected a standard 12-color palette that simply complement my decade-old [Kubuntu desktop](https://store.kde.org/p/1980663)[^4]. [^4]: KDE, 30 years later, still going strong! ![](https://images.pling.com/img/00/00/51/57/23/1980663/screenshot-20230201-205024.png){.lightbox} Another remarkable tool I have used in the past to generate sensible UI color schemes is [themer.dev](https://themer.dev/)[^5] -- this online masterpiece will generate consistent color schemes for Linux desktops and for many consoles, text editors, and IDEs. Check it out! [^5]: Development environment theme creator ![](themer.png){.lightbox} ```{.r .cell-code} library(htmltools) pal <- c( cyan = "#789494", teal = "#445e64", dark = "#222e32", pink = "#aea39a", purple = "#98796f", indigo = "#9b59b6", blue = "#3daee9", green = "#27ae60", yellow = "#edcd37", orange = "#f67400", red = "#da4453", light = "#eff0f1" ) n <- c(rep(2,6), rep(4,6)) lapply(1:length(pal), function(i) div(class=paste0( "g-col-", n[i], " small rounded text-center p-2 bg-", names(pal)[i]), HTML(names(pal)[i], "

``` # Block Elements Simple indented blockquote with end credits. > Blockquote title\ > Blockquote content comes here...\ > -- Author Bootstrap built-in **callout block** and **card** components are readily available in Quarto Markdown with the usual semantic colors. ::: callout Note that there are 6 types of callout blocks, including: `default`, `note`, `warning`, `important`, `tip`, and `caution`. This is the **default** callout style. ::: ::: callout-note This is a **note**. ::: ``` markdown ::: callout-tip ### Callout title This is an example of a **tip** callout with a title. ::: ``` ::: callout-tip ### Callout title This is an example of a **tip** with a title. ::: ``` markdown ::: callout-caution collapse="true" ### Expand to learn about collapse This is an example of a 'collapsible' **caution** callout ::: ``` ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ### Expand to learn about collapse This is an example of a collapsible **caution** callout box. You can use `collapse="true"` to collapse it by default or `collapse="false"` to make a collapsible callout that is expanded by default. ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Important"} This is a callout with a header title. ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Warning"} This is an **important** callout with a title. ::: # Typography Bootstrap default line-height and font sizing typically work, but I like to enforce a strict vertical grid whenever possible, so I make sure to define all vertical spacing and padding as multiple of a standard line height of `$spacer` (24px). ::: {.cell filename='./www/theme-mblabs.scss'} ```{.scss .cell-code} $spacer: 26px !default; $spacers: ( 0: 0, 1: $spacer * .25, 2: $spacer * .5, 3: $spacer * 1, 4: $spacer * 1.5, 5: $spacer * 2, ); $font-size-base: 1rem; // 17px in `_quarto.yml` $h1-font-size: calc($font-size-base + 15px); // 32px $h2-font-size: calc($font-size-base + 9px); // 26px $h3-font-size: calc($font-size-base + 11px); // 28px $h4-font-size: calc($font-size-base + 5px); // 22px $h5-font-size: calc($font-size-base + 3px); // 20px $h6-font-size: calc($font-size-base); $line-height-base: calc($spacer / 17px); $headings-line-height: $line-height-base; $list-inline-padding: .5* $spacer; ``` ::: No additional changes to font definitions aside from using `Source Sans Pro`, `Oswald`, and `Roboto Condensed` fonts. This is how **bold**, *italic*, and smaller text spans. Here is ^superscript^ and ~subscript~ text, and ~~strikethrough~~ notes. Semantic colors with e.g. [.text-info]{.text-info} provide accented text. I have added 2 background classes for my own use, a semi-transparent and blurred [`.shaded`]{.shaded} and a [`.striped`]{.striped}. I use [.text-muted]{.text-muted} for all post metadata, end and margin notes, and for captioning. ## Heading 2 Sample paragraph content. ### Heading 3 Sample paragraph content with list of items: - List 1 - List 2 - List 3 Ordered list: 1. "lines"), legend.key.size = unit(0.85, "lines"), legend.text = element_text(size=base_size*0.95, hjust=0), legend.position="top", legend.justification=0, legend.direction="horizontal", ... ) ``` ::: Next I apply (slightly opinionated) changes to `ggthemes::theme_foundation()`, mostly transparent fills, condensed font, simplified axes, and a y-axis on the right side. These graphic customizations are documented in `./R/theme.R` in this repo. This helps with handling dependencies and because I want to use them more flexibly across my blog posts. Obviously when visualizing scientific and spatial datasets the choice of color scales would require additional care. ::: {.cell filename='./R/theme.R'} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show function"} gglabs <- function( data = NULL, mapping = aes(), pos_x = c("bottom", "top"), pos_y = c("right", "left"), ...) { pos_x = match.arg(pos_x) pos_y = match.arg(pos_y) options( ggplot2.discrete.colour = scale_labs_dc, ggplot2.discrete.fill = scale_labs_df, ggplot2.continuous.colour = scale_labs_cc, ggplot2.continuous.fill = scale_labs_cf ) ggplot(data, mapping ) + guides( x = if(pos_x=="top") guide_none() else guide_axis(), x.sec = if(pos_x=="bottom") guide_none() else guide_axis(), y = if(pos_y=="right") guide_none() else guide_axis(), y.sec = if(pos_y=="left") guide_none() else guide_axis() ) + theme_labs(...) } ``` ::: Below we generate a couple of categorical and continuous `ggplot` and `lattice` charts to make sure that everything looks adequate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Apply and check my new graphic theme library(mblabs) library(ggplot2) ``` ::: ::: {.cell .preview-image} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(carb), mpg, fill=factor(carb))) + geom_col() + scale_labs_df(name="carb") + guides(y=guide_none(), y.sec=guide_axis()) + labs( title="My Long and Descriptive Plot Title", subtitle="My very long subtitle with many units", caption="My very long plot caption with many references.") + theme_labs() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png) ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_smooth(color=pal["orange"], fill=pal["pink"]) + geom_point(size=3, aes(color=carb)) + scale_labs_cc() + guides(y=guide_none(), y.sec=guide_axis()) + labs( title="My Long and Descriptive Plot Title", subtitle="My very long subtitle with many units", caption="My very long plot caption with many references.") + theme_labs() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png) ::: ::: Instead of applyng `theme_set(theme_labs())` globally, I prefer to use a custom ggplot function `gglabs()` that also modifies X and Y guides. Note that the code chunk below will produce a PNG instead of SVG file. I also set a resolution of `knitr fig-dpi: 220` globally in `_quarto.yml` so plots still look adequate when printed to paper. ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| fig-format: png gglabs(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, z=density)) + geom_raster(aes(fill=density)) + geom_contour(color=pal["cyan"]) ``` ```` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png) ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gglabs(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, color=factor(cyl))) + geom_point(size=4) + labs(title="My Title", subtitle="My Subtitle", caption="My plot caption") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png) ::: ::: Similarly we make changes to lattice `par()` options. This is important as many advanced statistical and spatial libraries continue to favor base R `graphics` library. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lattice::show.settings() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A sample histogram in base R to demo my new color scheme](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png) ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <- rchisq(100, df=4) hist(x, freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 0.2), col=1:11, border=12, xlab=NA) grid(NA, NULL, col=4) curve(dchisq(x, df=4), col=2, lty=2, lwd=2, add=TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A sample histogram in base R to demo my new color scheme](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-2.png) ::: ::: # Publishing Workflow The latest Quarto release adds perfectly sensible options to optimize everyone's publishing workflow, in particular through the use of **Draft** and **Freeze** behavior: - `draft: true` Tells Quarto that a document may (or may not) be listed / accessible to viewers, and prevents automatic re-tangling. - `freeze: true` Tells Quarto to only re-tangle a document on content change, and not every time a site is rebuilt.
